The regression guard tests/plugin/unit/test_proposal_service.py::test_staging_creates_private_directories_all_the_way_down walks from XDG_STATE_HOME down through techtree-hermes to the run directory and asserts 0700 at each level, with the staged SKILL.md at 0600. Ticket techtree-python-oj8 stays open pending chief verification.

finding_disposition.finding: The guided revision spends the host's money through the host's own model, and Techtree cannot see what it cost. Worse, the host can bill for an answer that contains nothing: on 2026-08-20 a completion spent its whole 32,768-token ceiling in the reasoning channel, returned message.content null, billed USD 0.1589, and the product counted the user's one revision as used with the typed code host_llm_unavailable — which is untrue, because the host answered and charged for it.
finding_disposition.future_ticket: techtree-python-bbu, with the design work in techtree-python-cjj
finding_disposition.risk: a first-time user pays for a completion and receives nothing, with no second attempt. This has now happened twice in acceptance, for two unrelated reasons.
finding_disposition.scope: the one guided revision the v0.1 introduction allows. It does not touch the comparison path, whose spend is bounded and pre-checked (cost bound USD 2.4152 against a declared maximum of 2.5).
finding_disposition.why_accepted: the host owns the sampling stack, the ceiling and the billing relationship; Techtree is handed one call and told nothing about its price. Metering it would mean claiming knowledge the product does not have. The plugin records the attempt honestly and the dossier states the division out loud rather than implying coverage: 'What Hermes does inside the single call it is handed is recorded per attempt and left to the host to account for — we do not claim more than we can hold.' The trigger is profile-specific; the consequence is not.

finding_disposition.finding: doctor reports the evaluation model credential PASS on presence and shape alone (verifiers/credentials.py:101-141, doctor/execution_checks.py:233). A revoked, expired or wrong-team key passes.
finding_disposition.risk: the exact failure the check exists to prevent — a run that looks configured, provisions Docker, and finds thirty seconds later that nothing can answer.
finding_disposition.scope: the pre-run readiness check only. Nothing downstream trusts it further.
finding_disposition.why_accepted: validating the key means spending a request against the provider from inside a readiness check, which is its own unwelcome surprise, and a free introspection endpoint is provider-specific. The failure when it comes is loud and typed, and it arrives before any episode completes, so the cost is a stopped run rather than a wrong result. The check is also careful about the thing it can get wrong cheaply: it answers for the environment a detached run would be given, not for the terminal it was typed into.

finding_disposition.disposition: ACCEPTED for v0.1 as a documentation fix
finding_disposition.finding: The published install argv lets uv choose the interpreter. On a machine whose default is 3.14 it installs onto CPython 3.14.7, outside the wheel's declared Requires-Python: >=3.12,<3.14, and the user's first doctor fails with 'Python 3.14.7 is outside the supported range'.
finding_disposition.risk: a first-run failure on a machine that is otherwise fine. It is the first thing a new user would see.
finding_disposition.scope: the published install instructions, and only on machines defaulting to 3.14
finding_disposition.why_accepted: nothing is wrong with the product: the wheel metadata is correct, the doctor detects the condition, names it precisely and refuses. What is wrong is one line of published copy. Pinning --python 3.12 in the quickstart fixes it without a code change, which makes it a docs ticket rather than a release blocker.

finding_disposition.disposition: ACCEPTED — and it is the outcome that was asked for

finding_disposition.future_ticket: techtree-python-llv (closed; the appeal to Nous Research is outstanding)
finding_disposition.risk: a reader who confirms without reading gets the same install as a reader who reads. The five findings are inherent to what the plugin is: a command-word list that constitutes a guard, three fixed-argv calls to a pinned CLI, and a control-character stripper matched by a rule looking for obfuscation.
finding_disposition.scope: plugin installation, until trusted-source or verified-publisher status is granted
finding_disposition.why_accepted: the alternative paths were both refused and remain refused: no fixture was disguised, renamed or encoded to slip past a scanner, and nothing anywhere tells a user or an agent to switch scanning off. What was done instead is real — the adversarial corpus moved out of the installable tree, taking the verdict from DANGEROUS with no override to CAUTION with a confirm — and the onboarding copy now states the verdict in advance, explains each finding in plain words and says the scanning stays on.

finding_disposition.disposition: ACCEPTED — recorded per contract §'Plugin Skill conflict scan'
finding_disposition.finding: The plugin's envelope-conflict scan is deterministic and statement-level. A paraphrase can pass it. v0.1 adds no LLM-based semantic scanner.
finding_disposition.risk: an operator Skill could carry an instruction that conflicts with the safety envelope in words the scan does not match.
finding_disposition.scope: future untrusted operator Skills. In v0.1 the only inputs are two digest-pinned founder Skills and one model-authored revision that a person sees before anything happens with it.
finding_disposition.why_accepted: four things hold instead, and none of them is the scan: the founder Skills are pinned by exact digest and byte-identical across three repositories; there is a manual security review; there are negative tests for known conflicting instructions; and the envelope is hardcoded — one-turn, no-upload and no-auto-run are not expressible in a Skill and cannot be overridden by one. An LLM scanner would put a model in the position of deciding whether another model's output is safe, which is a larger design question than v0.1 should answer in passing.

finding_disposition.disposition: ACCEPTED — founder ruling, recorded here for completeness
finding_disposition.finding: Two deterministic guards on the guided-revision path were deleted by founder ruling: the numeric-claims heuristic (techtree-python-5f6) and the generic secret-assignment heuristic (techtree-python-0mx).
finding_disposition.risk: less deterministic checking of model-authored text than the design originally carried.
finding_disposition.scope: the guided-revision narrative and Skill-scan paths
finding_disposition.why_accepted: both were destroying paid turns on ordinary English — 'modulo-97' read as the number -97 on a task family about arithmetic modulo 97, and 'that token: no reasoning' read as a credential assignment on a Climb entirely about returning a token. Neither guard held the envelope; both guessed at meaning from surface text. The envelope itself, the copy-guard and the Skill scanner's structural rules are untouched, and ndq.3.28 strengthened the copy-guard in the same cycle.

finding_disposition.finding: Two of the seven contract scrubber cases have no test: token in query string (neither scrubber) and private key block (Python side). Both redact today; both were verified by hand for this review.
finding_disposition.risk: the behaviour is not held by anything. On the Python side the query-string case is caught incidentally by the secret-assignment rule rather than by a rule written for it, and the PEM case is caught by the opaque-run rule, which leaves the BEGIN/END framing and would leave a final body line under 40 characters.
finding_disposition.scope: error-message and error-details scrubbing on both sides of the CLI boundary
finding_disposition.why_accepted: no case leaks, which is the stop condition. Adding two tests is a small, safe change, but it is a change to the certified tree at the end of the release, and the measured behaviour is recorded here so nothing rests on an untested assumption being invisible.

finding_disposition.finding: Both recursive scrubbers walk str, mapping and list. A tuple or set passes through with its secret intact.
finding_disposition.risk: an unscrubbed credential in an error's details, if such a shape ever arrives
finding_disposition.scope: error details on both sides
finding_disposition.why_accepted: unreachable through the shapes that exist. On the Python side sanitize_details is typed JsonValue under strict mypy, so an authored call site cannot pass a tuple. On the plugin side the input is a JSON-decoded envelope and json.loads produces no tuples. It is one refactor away from being reachable, which is why it is written down rather than left as a detail.

finding_disposition.disposition: ACCEPTED — this is the design, and it is why the claim is narrow

finding_disposition.disposition: ACCEPTED — and this is precisely why the contract requires three methods

No single one of them carries the claim.

method_3_destination_capture.what_samples_are: polling cycles, not requests. Each is one lsof sweep over the journey's process tree. 884 samples is 884 snapshots, and the union of what they saw is five addresses.

kill_injection.method: containers identified by before/after id diff with the exact ids recorded at the moment of the kill, never by image. No forced container removal and no sweep: the only cleanup path exercised is the supervisor's SIGTERM to the eval's own process group and the pinned engine's own teardown.
kill_injection.no_report_and_no_proof: a SIGKILLed worker cannot write its own terminal state, so no report directory and no proof bundle were produced. A killed comparison yields no result, which is the point.

cases.note: caught incidentally on the Python side by the secret-assignment pattern rather than by a rule written for it. Working, but nothing would notice if it stopped.

guard_deletion_history.honest_reading: the deterministic surface is smaller than it was, and what is gone was the part that produced false positives rather than the part that held the envelope. The paraphrase gap is unchanged by the deletions: it was there before them and it is there now.

stop_conditions.evidence: release/network-method-log.json: the product made one techtree.sh request across its whole non-paid command surface and its method was GET. src/techtree/skills/starter.py:375-376 hardcodes method='GET' and is the package's only outbound call site. The ash release surface answers POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE on every published address with 405 (lib/techtree_web/method_surface.ex:26-47, 11 paths × 4 verbs asserted at test/techtree_web/router_test.exs:64-91).

an AST scan of every module in src/techtree finds exactly two network imports, both urllib, both in skills/starter.py:53-54. The CLI's lock resolves 37 packages and contains no HTTP client at all. No POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE call site exists. The verifiers uploader is upstream's and is proved not loaded: tests/preflight/test_verifiers_eval_contract.py:405 asserts verifiers.v1.utils.platform never enters sys.modules on a complete run with a credential present, and :422 is the control that proves the probe can fire.

engine.note: the engine is where HTTP clients live, and that is the design: the CLI never depends on Verifiers, and the engine is installed into its own environment. verifiers_push.argv: src/techtree/verifiers/child.py:105 PUSH_DISABLED_FLAG = '--no-push', emitted on the real eval argv at :163 and on the dry-run argv at :179. A flag on argv overrides whatever the file says, so the two layers are belt and braces rather than one restated.
verifiers_push.compiled_config: src/techtree/verifiers/config.py:258 — push: Literal[False] = False. A configuration that spells push = true is unrepresentable, not merely defaulted away. Constructed at src/techtree/verifiers/compiler.py:171.
